claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for targeting brain regions, illustrated in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: At the conclusion of the experiment, some monkeys received retrograde tracer injections at the same sites targeted by the drug infusions.
claims.source: In addition, at the conclusion of the experiment, some monkeys received retrograde tracer injections at the same sites targeted by the drug infusions (Figure 2b–d).
claims.evidence: This describes a verification procedure, illustrated in Figure 2b-d.

claims.claim: Retrograde tracer injections allowed verification that the infusion sites identified by structural MR scans at the beginning of the experiment were as intended throughout the study.
claims.source: This allowed us to verify that the infusion sites identified by structural MR scans at the beginning of the experiment were as intended throughout the study.
claims.evidence: This describes the purpose of the tracer injections.

claims.claim: A within-subjects design was used in which each of five monkeys received infusions of THIP or saline within area 13 and area 11, both before and after selective satiation.
claims.source: We used a within-subjects design. Each of five monkeys received infusions of THIP or saline within area 13 and, in separate sessions, area 11, both before and after selective satiation.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: Sites in areas 13 and 11 were roughly 5 mm apart in the anteroposterior dimension.
claims.source: Sites in areas 13 and 11 were roughly 5 mm apart in the anteroposterior dimension (Figure 1c,d).
claims.evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between infusion sites, illustrated in Figure 1c,d.

claims.claim: The reinforcer devaluation was conducted repeatedly, with a minimum of one week between selective satiation procedures.
claims.source: To collect these data, the reinforcer devaluation was conducted repeatedly, with a minimum of one week between selective satiation procedures.
claims.evidence: This describes the temporal structure of the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: When saline was infused into either area 13 or 11, the monkeys showed robust devaluation effects.
claims.source: As expected, when saline was infused into either area 13 or 11 the monkeys showed robust devaluation effects (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a control result showing normal behavior, illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: After selective satiation, monkeys shifted their choices to images that yielded the higher value outcome when saline was infused.
claims.source: That is, after selective satiation, monkeys shifted their choices to images that yielded the higher value outcome.
claims.evidence: This describes the normal devaluation effect observed in control conditions.

claims.claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant three-way interaction between Treatment, Region, and Time, indicating that behavioral effects of inactivation differed both as a function of area and of timing.
claims.source: A repeated-measures ANOVA on proportion shifted with factors of Treatment (THIP, saline), Region (area 13, area 11), and Time (before satiation, after satiation) revealed a significant three-way interaction (F(1,4) = 16.82, p = 0.015, partial η2 = 0.81), indicating that behavioral effects of inactivation differed both as a function of area and of timing.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the main experiment.

claims.claim: Post-hoc tests revealed a double dissociation of function within the OFC.
claims.source: Post-hoc tests, detailed below, revealed a double dissociation of function within the OFC.
claims.evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by statistical analyses.

claims.claim: When monkeys selected goals based on updated subjective valuations, inactivation of area 13 but not area 11 during the value-updating phase caused an impairment.
claims.source: When monkeys selected goals based on updated subjective valuations, inactivation of area 13 but not area 11 during the value-updating phase caused an impairment.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the post-hoc tests.

claims.claim: Inactivation of area 11 but not area 13 during the goal-selection phase of the experiment caused an impairment.
claims.source: In contrast, inactivation of area 11 but not area 13 during the goal-selection phase of the experiment caused an impairment.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the post-hoc tests.

claims.claim: Scores obtained when saline was infused before selective satiation did not differ from those obtained when saline was infused after selective satiation.
claims.source: Scores obtained when saline was infused before selective satiation did not differ from those obtained when saline was infused after selective satiation (repeated-measures ANOVA with factors of Region and Time; for all main effects and interactions: F(1,4) < 1.48, p > 0.29); we therefore pooled saline data within each region for subsequent analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result justifying the pooling of control data.

claims.claim: THIP infusions into area 13 before satiation significantly lowered proportion shifted scores relative to those obtained with saline infusions.
claims.source: Planned follow-up comparisons revealed that THIP infusions into area 13 before satiation significantly lowered proportion shifted scores relative to those obtained with saline infusions (two-tailed paired t-tests with Bonferroni-corrected alpha = 0.025 for all follow-up tests; t4 = 5.61, p = 0.005, d = 2.51).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the main experiment.

claims.claim: Infusions of THIP into area 13 after satiation had no effect on proportion shifted scores.
claims.source: Infusions of THIP into area 13 after satiation had no effect (t4 = 0.24, p = 0.826).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the main experiment.

claims.claim: Area 13 appears to be essential for value updating but not for selecting visual goals based on that information.
claims.source: Because normal functioning of area 13 was necessary during, but not after, satiation, area 13 appears to be essential for value updating but not for selecting visual goals based on that information (Figure 4, left).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: THIP infusions into area 11 before satiation had no effect on behavior.
claims.source: THIP infusions into area 11 before satiation had no effect on behavior (t4 = 0.44, p = 0.686), whereas THIP infusions after satiation disrupted devaluation effects (t4 = 4.36, p = 0.012, d = 1.95).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the main experiment.

claims.claim: THIP infusions into area 11 after satiation disrupted devaluation effects.
claims.source: THIP infusions into area 11 before satiation had no effect on behavior (t4 = 0.44, p = 0.686), whereas THIP infusions after satiation disrupted devaluation effects (t4 = 4.36, p = 0.012, d = 1.95).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the main experiment.

claims.claim: Area 11 appears to be essential for advantageous goal selection but not value updating.
claims.source: Thus, area 11 appears to be essential for advantageous goal selection but not value updating (Figure 4, right).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The same pattern of results was found when using proportion choices of images associated with the nonsated food as the dependent measure.
claims.source: We also conducted the analysis using proportion choices of images associated with the nonsated food as the dependent measure, and found the same pattern of results (area 13, pre-sate vs. saline: t4 = 5.95, p = 0.004, d = 2.66, post-sate vs. saline: t4 = − 0.14, p = 0.898; area 11, pre-sate vs. saline: t4 = 0.46, p = 0.669, post-sate vs. saline: t4 = 4.72, p = 0.009, d = 2.11).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming the main findings using an alternative measure.

claims.claim: In the absence of satiation, infusions of THIP into either area 11 or area 13 did not change monkeys' choices of images paired with each food type.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5A, in the absence of satiation, infusions of THIP into either area did not change monkeys' choices of images paired with each food type (repeated-measures ANOVA; F(2,8) = 0.06, p = 0.945).
claims.evidence: This is a control result illustrated in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The lack of effect of THIP infusions in the absence of satiation, together with other control results, rules out the possibility that infusion of THIP, per se, disrupted monkeys' choices.
claims.source: These data, together with the lack of effect of THIP infusions either after selective satiation in area 13 or before selective satiation in area 11 (Figure 4), rules out the possibility that infusion of THIP, per se, disrupted monkeys' choices.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the control results.

claims.claim: THIP infusions into area 11 before test sessions did not affect accuracy on the familiar 60 image pairs.
claims.source: THIP infusions into area 11 before test sessions did not affect accuracy on the familiar 60 image pairs (t3 < 0.001, p > 0.999; Figure 5B), response speed on correct trials (median response latencies, mean (SEM); no-drug baseline = 1.53 s (0.17); THIP infusion before = 1.35 s (0.17); t3 = 1.45, p = 0.242), or time to complete test sessions (total session duration, mean (SD); no-drug baseline = 449.8 s (46.69); THIP infusion before = 468.1 s (54.92); t3 = 1.63, p = 0.201).
claims.evidence: This is a control result illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: THIP infusions into area 11 after selective satiation specifically disrupted retrieval or use of the recently updated value, as opposed to having a general effect on choosing rewarded images.
claims.source: These data, together with the lack of effect of inactivation of area 11 in our first control procedure, described above, led us to conclude that THIP infusions into area 11 after selective satiation in our main task specifically disrupted retrieval or use of the recently updated value, as opposed to having a general effect on choosing rewarded images.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the control results.

claims.claim: When monkeys could choose between visible foods directly, rather than choosing between images that had previously been paired with food, THIP infusions had no effect on choices.
claims.source: When monkeys could choose between visible foods directly, rather than choosing between images that had previously been paired with food, THIP infusions had no effect on choices, regardless of whether that was measured as a function of proportion shifted, as used for image choices, or as a function of the proportion choice of the nonsated food (repeated-measures ANOVA with factors of region and treatment; for all main effects of region: F(1,2) < 8.68, p > 0.098; for all main effects of treatment and interactions: F(2,4) < 0.29, p > 0.764; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a control result illustrated in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The reversible inactivations had no discernable influence on satiety mechanisms, and the selective satiation procedure produced the desired effect.
claims.source: Thus, consistent with our earlier work based on permanent lesions (Izquierdo et al., 2004; Rudebeck et al., 2013), the reversible inactivations had no discernable influence on satiety mechanisms, and the selective satiation procedure produced the desired effect.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the control results, supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The results reveal a double dissociation of function between the anterior and posterior components of the OFC, areas 11 and 13.
claims.source: Our results reveal a double dissociation of function between the anterior and posterior components of the OFC, areas 11 and 13, which Carmichael and Price (1996) characterize as components of an orbitomedial prefrontal 'sensory network'.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: The mutually supportive and complementary functions of areas 11 and 13 agree with the concept of an orbitomedial prefrontal 'sensory network'.
claims.source: Their mutually supportive and complementary functions agree with this concept of prefrontal organization.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation relating the findings to existing theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: When an outcome's value is altered, area 13—but not area 11—is essential for a value updating function.
claims.source: When an outcome's value is altered, area 13—but not area 11—is essential for a value updating function.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claims.claim: After updating has occurred, area 11—but not area 13—is essential for translating the knowledge about current valuations into advantageous choices.
claims.source: After updating has occurred, however, area 11—but not area 13—is essential for translating the knowledge about current valuations into advantageous choices.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claims.claim: Areas 11 and 13 play complementary roles in mediating devaluation effects: the caudal part of the OFC updates valuations and the rostral part translates this knowledge into action.
claims.source: Thus, these two areas play complementary roles in mediating devaluation effects: the caudal part of the OFC updates valuations and the rostral part translates this knowledge into action.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claims.claim: The present experiment provides the first demonstration of a double dissociation of function between the anterior and posterior components of the primate OFC.
claims.source: The present experiment provides the first demonstration of a double dissociation of function between the anterior and posterior components of the primate OFC, which complements recent studies that have pointed to functional differences between its medial and lateral parts (Bouret and Richmond, 2010; Noonan et al., 2010; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, supported by citations to related work.

claims.claim: The finding of an impairment when area 11 was inactivated after—but not before—the selective satiation procedure is particularly significant.
claims.source: The finding of an impairment when area 11 was inactivated after—but not before—the selective satiation procedure is particularly significant.
claims.evidence: This is an evaluative statement about the importance of a specific finding.

claims.claim: The monkeys had acquired information about the new, updated value of the food outcome, yet their choices did not reflect this when area 11 was inactivated after satiation.
claims.source: The monkeys had by all indications acquired information about the new, updated value of the food outcome, yet their choices did not reflect this.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Area 11 is not necessary for updating valuations per se, but rather for the use of this knowledge to choose goals based on visual stimuli associated with predicted food outcomes.
claims.source: This observation shows that area 11 is not necessary for updating valuations per se, but rather for the use of this knowledge to choose goals based on visual stimuli associated with predicted food outcomes.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Once value updating has occurred, area 11 plays the dominant role and area 13 is no longer needed to guide choices between stimuli based on current valuations.
claims.source: In essence, once value updating has occurred, area 11 plays the dominant role and area 13 is no longer needed to guide choices between stimuli based on current valuations.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Storage of the updated value occurred either during or shortly after the selective satiation procedure, a process that depended on area 13.
claims.source: Presumably, storage of the updated value occurred either during or shortly after the selective satiation procedure, a process that depended on area 13, and this information was then broadcast to other areas, including area 11.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claims.claim: Inactivation of area 11 immediately before the probe tests prevented the optimal use of updated value knowledge.
claims.source: Inactivation of area 11 immediately before the probe tests prevented the optimal use of this knowledge.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Infusion of similar volumes of THIP into the pulvinar produced behavioral effects in monkeys lasting several hours.
claims.source: Infusion of similar volumes of THIP into the pulvinar produced behavioral effects in monkeys lasting several hours (Wilke et al., 2013), and smaller volumes administered in rat superior colliculus affected behavior for at least two hours (Di Scala et al., 1983), both well beyond the elapsed time between pre-satiation infusion and choice tests in the present study.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on THIP duration of action.

claims.claim: The negative results after pre-satiation infusions probably reflect the cooperative function of other prefrontal areas.
claims.source: Instead, our negative results after pre-satiation infusions probably reflect the cooperative function of other prefrontal areas, which would also explain the relatively mild effect of choice-phase area 11 inactivations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: The impairment when area 11 was inactive only during goal selection, but not when it was inactive during both value updating and goal selection, suggests that area 11 plays a dominant role in a partially-redundant goal-selection network.
claims.source: The impairment when area 11 was inactive only during goal selection, but not when it was inactive during both value updating and goal selection, suggests that area 11 plays a dominant role in a partially-redundant goal-selection network.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: When area 11 was inactivated before the selective satiation procedure, it was effectively taken 'offline', rendering it unable to receive updated valuation signals and therefore unable to participate in goal selection later.
claims.source: Another possibility is that when area 11 was inactivated before the selective satiation procedure, it was effectively taken 'offline', rendering it unable to receive updated valuation signals and therefore unable to participate in goal selection later.
claims.evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: When area 11 had received updated valuation signals during the satiation procedure it made a significant contribution to goal selection, but otherwise did not.
claims.source: According to this account, when area 11 had received updated valuation signals during the satiation procedure it made a significant contribution to goal selection, but otherwise did not.
claims.evidence: This is part of an alternative speculative interpretation.

claims.claim: Neighboring prefrontal areas could mediate goal selection when area 11 was inactivated before satiation.
claims.source: Presumably, neighboring prefrontal areas could mediate goal selection in this circumstance.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claims.claim: Inactivation of area 13 yielded a pattern of results virtually identical to that observed after inactivation of basolateral amygdala in monkeys performing the same task.
claims.source: Notably, inactivation of area 13 yielded a pattern of results virtually identical to that observed after inactivation of basolateral amygdala in monkeys performing the same task (Wellman et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The present results point to an interaction of the basolateral amygdala with area 13 to support value updating, specifically during the selective satiation procedure.
claims.source: Given the evidence from neuropsychological studies that the amygdala and the OFC must functionally interact in mediating devaluation effects (Baxter et al., 2000), the present results point to an interaction of the basolateral amygdala with area 13 to support value updating, specifically during the selective satiation procedure.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in light of previous findings, supported by citation.

claims.claim: During normal devaluation, values get updated gradually during the selective satiation procedure.
claims.source: One implication of this result is that, during normal devaluation, values get updated gradually during the selective satiation procedure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The effect of satiation might be computed (read-in) at the time of the choice, rather than areas involved in goal selection receiving real-time information about gradual devaluation.
claims.source: This does not imply, however, that the areas involved in goal selection receive real-time information about this gradual devaluation. Instead, from a modeling perspective, the effect of satiation might be computed (read-in) at the time of the choice.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the computational mechanism.

claims.claim: Area 13, specifically area 13m, is the first site of convergence in the OFC of gustatory, olfactory, somatic, visceral, and visual sensory inputs.
claims.source: Area 13, specifically area 13m, is the first site of convergence in the OFC of gustatory, olfactory, somatic, visceral, and visual sensory inputs.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical claim supported by citations.

claims.claim: Area 13 has been proposed to be the site of sensory representations of food outcomes, including the sensory properties of the food as well as its value.
claims.source: On these grounds, it has been proposed to be the site of sensory representations of food outcomes, including the sensory properties of the food as well as its value (Carmichael and Price, 1996; Critchley and Rolls, 1996; Rolls, 2000; Saleem et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Neurons in area 13 of macaques recorded during performance of reward-guided tasks signal the value and identity of expected outcomes.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, neurons in area 13 of macaques recorded during performance of reward-guided tasks signal the value and identity of expected outcomes (Tremblay and Schultz, 1999; Wallis and Miller, 2003; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; 2008; 2009), as do neurons in the amygdala (Paton et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to electrophysiological studies.

claims.claim: The pattern of results is consistent with functional imaging studies showing a role for the human OFC in signaling changes in food value specific to the food consumed.
claims.source: The pattern of results we observed is consistent with functional imaging studies showing a role for the human OFC in signaling changes in food value specific to the food consumed (Small et al., 2001; Gottfried et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claims.claim: Either during or soon after the value updating process, the new value is transmitted from area 13 to area 11 and potentially to other prefrontal cortical regions as well.
claims.source: Apparently, either during or soon after the value updating process, the new value is transmitted from area 13 to area 11 and potentially to other prefrontal cortical regions as well.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Area 13 is not an essential part of the circuitry generating goals for action.
claims.source: The fact that area 13 does not need to be active during the choice phase reveals that area 13 is not an essential part of the circuitry generating goals for action.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Human fMRI studies suggest that the anterior OFC may represent foods at an abstract level.
claims.source: Human fMRI studies suggest that the anterior OFC may represent foods at an abstract level; the posterior OFC in humans is more active in response to pictures of food relative to nonfood objects (van der Laan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human neuroimaging study.

claims.claim: Klein-Flugge et al. (2013) proposed that the anterior OFC, in the region of area 11, houses a stimulus–food outcome representation, whereas the more posterior OFC, in the region of area 13, houses representations of reward identity, independent of associated stimuli.
claims.source: Based on BOLD changes consequent to sensory-specific adaptation, Klein-Flugge et al. (2013) proposed that the anterior OFC, in the region of area 11, houses a stimulus–food outcome representation, whereas the more posterior OFC, in the region of area 13, houses representations of reward identity, independent of associated stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klein-Flugge et al. (2013).

claims.claim: The pattern of results from Klein-Flugge et al. (2013) is consistent with the present findings, but leaves unanswered how visual sensory input translates this knowledge into goals.
claims.source: This pattern of results is consistent with our findings, but leaves unanswered how visual sensory input translates this knowledge into goals.
claims.evidence: This is an evaluation of how previous findings relate to the current study.

claims.claim: Because area 11 can mediate adaptive choices independently of area 13, area 11 and associated circuits link visual inputs with the current, updated value of particular food outcomes.
claims.source: Because area 11 can mediate adaptive choices independently of area 13, we conclude that area 11 and associated circuits link visual inputs with the current, updated value of particular food outcomes.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The linking of visual inputs with current, updated value could occur within area 11, or it could occur in concert with anatomically related areas such as the ventral lateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC), area 12.
claims.source: This could occur within area 11, or it could occur in concert with anatomically related areas such as the ventral lateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC), area 12, a region known to be important for visual attentional selection (Rushworth et al., 2005) and for switching among competing behavior-guiding rules (Bussey et al., 2001; Rossi et al., 2007; Baxter et al., 2009; Buckley et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies of area 12 function.

claims.claim: West et al. (2011) found that bilateral inactivation of the OFC disrupted both value updating and goal selection based on those valuations.
claims.source: West et al. (2011) have performed an experiment like the present one and found that bilateral inactivation of the OFC disrupted both value updating and goal selection based on those valuations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to West et al. (2011).

claims.source: Because they infused muscimol into a central location within the OFC, their infusions probably affected both areas 11 and 13 simultaneously, which accounts for the difference between their results and ours.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation explaining differences between studies.

claims.claim: Anatomical studies have suggested a hierarchical organization in the anteroposterior dimension of the OFC.
claims.source: Anatomical studies have suggested a hierarchical organization in the anteroposterior dimension of the OFC.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about anatomical organization, supported by subsequent citations.

claims.claim: By analogy with sensory corticocortical connections, the posteriorly-directed projections within the OFC are said to follow a 'feedforward' projection pattern characterized by projections that arise in supragranular layers (layers 2–3) of the cortex.
claims.source: Specifically, by analogy with sensory corticocortical connections, the posteriorly-directed projections within the OFC are said to follow a "feedforward" projection pattern characterized by projections that arise in supragranular layers (layers 2–3) of the cortex (Carmichael and Price, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carmichael and Price (1996).

claims.claim: The preponderance of cells giving rise to the posteriorly-directed projections from area 11 to area 13 and from area 13 to the agranular insular cortex arise from layers 2 and 3.
claims.source: For example, the preponderance of cells giving rise to the posteriorly-directed projections from area 11 to area 13 and, likewise, from area 13 to the agranular insular cortex, arise from layers 2 and 3.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical claim about the laminar origin of projections.

claims.claim: The anatomical picture is consistent with a model in which visual sensory representations in area 11 subsequently activate representations in more posterior areas, where they become integrated with updated value signals.
claims.source: This picture is consistent with a model in which visual sensory representations in area 11 subsequently activate representations in more posterior areas, where they become integrated with updated value signals.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on anatomical data.

claims.claim: When area 13 is inactive during the probe tests, other regions, such as area 12 of the VLPFC or the anterior insula, are sufficient to provide the information about updated value.
claims.source: When area 13 is inactive during the probe tests, however, other regions, such as area 12 of the VLPFC or the anterior insula, are sufficient to provide the information about updated value.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: To influence behavior, the OFC must eventually affect the motor system.
claims.source: To influence behavior, the OFC must eventually affect the motor system.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about how the OFC influences behavior.

claims.claim: One model posits a serial model in which offer values are compared, perhaps in a common currency, the offer with the greater value is selected, and then an action is selected to implement that choice.
claims.source: One idea posits a serial model (Padoa-Schioppa, 2011) in which offer values are compared, perhaps in a common currency. The offer with the greater value is selected, and then an action is selected to implement that choice.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a theoretical model, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Another model suggests that value signals could influence processing in visuomotor pathways that plan movements through a mechanism akin to top–down attention and biased competition.
claims.source: Another model suggests that value signals could influence processing in visuomotor pathways that plan movements through a mechanism akin to top–down attention and biased competition (Pastor-Bernier and Cisek, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a description of an alternative theoretical model, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Influences of current value on choice might be mediated by connections between the OFC and the ventral, medial, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: By either model, these influences of current value on choice might be mediated by connections between the OFC and the ventral, medial, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Barbas and Pandya, 1989; Carmichael and Price, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about anatomical pathways, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The OFC and the VLPFC contribute to multisynaptic pathways to dorsal premotor areas, mainly via dorsal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: The OFC and the VLPFC contribute to multisynaptic pathways to dorsal premotor areas, mainly via dorsal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Takahara et al., 2012), and cingulate premotor areas, mainly via medial prefrontal cortex (Morecraft and Van Hoesen, 1998; Morecraft et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical claim supported by citations.

claims.claim: The VLPFC receives strong projections from areas 13 and 11 as well as from the basolateral amygdala.
claims.source: The VLPFC in particular receives strong projections from areas 13 and 11 as well as from the basolateral amygdala (Porrino et al., 1981; Saleem et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical claim supported by citations.

claims.claim: The OFC and the adjacent VLPFC are well situated to influence the selection of targets for action.
claims.source: Thus, the OFC and the adjacent VLPFC are well situated to influence the selection of targets for action.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical connectivity.

claims.claim: The posterior component of the macaque OFC, area 13, functions in conjunction with the basolateral amygdala to update the valuation of expected reward outcomes, based on an animal's current satiation state.
claims.source: The posterior component, area 13, functions in conjunction with the basolateral amygdala to update the valuation of expected reward outcomes, based on an animal's current satiation state.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: The anterior component of the macaque OFC, area 11, plays a critical role in translating knowledge about updated valuations into goals that produce an advantageous outcome.
claims.source: The anterior component, area 11, plays a critical role in translating this knowledge into goals that produce an advantageous outcome.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Area 11 is needed for choosing which of two visual stimuli to choose when both stimuli are abstractly associated with a particular reward outcome, but not for choices between two visible foods.
claims.source: Importantly, area 11 is needed for choosing which of two visual stimuli to choose when both stimuli are abstractly associated with a particular reward outcome, but not for choices between two visible foods.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The inability to translate abstract valuation knowledge into advantageous choices resembles the goal neglect that occurs after damage to the frontal lobe in humans.
claims.source: The inability to translate abstract valuation knowledge into advantageous choices resembles the goal neglect that occurs after damage to the frontal lobe in humans.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the findings to human neuropsychological phenomena.

results.result: Area 13 of the OFC is essential for value updating during selective satiation but not for subsequent goal selection. Inactivation of area 13 before satiation impaired devaluation effects (p=0.005, d=2.51), while inactivation after satiation had no effect (p=0.826).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C46, C49-C51 provide converging statistical evidence for a selective role of area 13 in value updating. The double dissociation design (C44-C45) with appropriate controls (C42-C43, C48, C56-C61) and significant effect sizes support this conclusion. The timing-dependent effects are well-documented.

results.result: Area 11 of the OFC is essential for goal selection based on updated valuations but not for value updating itself. Inactivation of area 11 after satiation impaired devaluation effects (p=0.012, d=1.95), while inactivation before satiation had no effect (p=0.686).
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C47, C52-C54 demonstrate the complementary role of area 11 through statistically significant effects with appropriate timing. The control experiments (C56-C61) rule out alternative explanations. The double dissociation with area 13 strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Areas 11 and 13 demonstrate a double dissociation of function within the OFC, with complementary roles in value-based goal selection. A significant three-way interaction (F(1,4)=16.82, p=0.015, η²=0.81) confirmed that inactivation effects differed by both area and timing.
results.evaluation: The double dissociation (C45, C62) is supported by the significant three-way interaction (C44) and converging evidence from both areas. The within-subjects design (C39) with appropriate controls strengthens causal inference. Claims C7, C28, C66-C67 appropriately interpret this pattern as complementary specialization.

results.result: Area 11 inactivation after satiation demonstrates goal neglect: monkeys acquired updated value knowledge but failed to translate it into advantageous choices. This resembles goal neglect observed in human frontal lobe patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 provide a mechanistic interpretation supported by the experimental data showing intact value updating but impaired choice behavior. The comparison to human goal neglect (C112) is reasonable given the behavioral parallels, though cross-species extrapolation requires caution. Control experiments (C58-C59) rule out general choice impairments.

results.result: Control experiments demonstrate that THIP infusions did not produce general behavioral impairments. Inactivation had no effect without satiation (p=0.945), on familiar discriminations (p>0.999), or on direct food choices (p>0.764).
results.evaluation: The three control procedures (C56, C58, C60) with non-significant results effectively rule out alternative explanations including general motor impairments, non-specific drug effects, and satiety mechanism disruption. Claims C57, C59, C61 appropriately interpret these null results as supporting the specificity of the main findings.

results.result: Area 13 inactivation produced effects virtually identical to amygdala inactivation in the same task, suggesting functional interaction between area 13 and the basolateral amygdala during value updating.
results.evaluation: The comparison to Wellman et al. (2005) findings (C16-C18, C80) is appropriate and strengthens the interpretation. The inference about amygdala-area 13 interaction (C81, C109) is supported by prior evidence of required functional interaction (C20) and the parallel timing-dependent effects.

results.result: Infusion sites were verified using structural MRI with gadolinium-saline and post-experiment retrograde tracer injections. Sites in areas 13 and 11 were approximately 5mm apart in the anteroposterior dimension.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 describe appropriate anatomical verification methods illustrated in Figure 2. The spatial separation (C40) is clearly documented in Figure 1c-d. These methodological details support the anatomical specificity of the manipulations.

results.result: The experimental design used within-subjects reversible inactivation with THIP before or after selective satiation to dissociate value updating from goal selection. Five monkeys received infusions in both areas 13 and 11 across repeated devaluation procedures.
results.evaluation: The methodological claims (C29-C35, C39, C41) accurately describe the experimental design illustrated in Figures 1 and 3. The within-subjects design with temporal manipulation provides appropriate control for dissociating the two processes. The logic linking timing to interpretation (C33, C35) is sound.

results.result: Saline infusions before versus after satiation produced equivalent effects, justifying pooling of control data. The main findings were replicated using an alternative dependent measure (proportion choice of nonsated food).
results.evaluation: The statistical justification for pooling saline conditions (C48) is appropriate given the non-significant differences. The replication with an alternative measure (C55) strengthens confidence in the findings, showing the results are not dependent on a specific scoring method.

results.result: The lack of impairment when area 11 was inactivated before satiation, despite expected drug persistence, suggests either compensatory function by other prefrontal areas or that area 11 must be active during satiation to receive updated value signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 present speculative interpretations of the unexpected null result. While C74 provides evidence for THIP duration, the competing explanations (C75-C79) remain untested hypotheses. The authors appropriately acknowledge this as speculation, but the mechanism remains unclear and would require additional experiments to resolve.

results.result: During normal devaluation, values are updated gradually during selective satiation, though the computational mechanism (real-time updating versus read-in at choice time) remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is a reasonable inference from the timing-dependent effects, but C83 acknowledges that the data do not distinguish between computational mechanisms. This represents an important limitation in mechanistic understanding that would require additional experiments (e.g., electrophysiology during satiation) to resolve.

results.result: Area 13 is proposed to be the site of sensory representations of food outcomes and their values, receiving multisensory inputs. Updated values are transmitted from area 13 to area 11 and other regions, but area 13 is not essential for generating action goals.
results.evaluation: The anatomical claims (C84) and functional proposals (C85-C86) are well-supported by citations. The inference that area 13 transmits updated values (C88) and is not essential for goal generation (C89) follows logically from the experimental results. The consistency with human imaging (C87) provides converging evidence.

results.result: Area 11 and associated circuits link visual inputs with current, updated values of food outcomes. This could occur within area 11 or in concert with ventral lateral prefrontal cortex (area 12).
results.evaluation: The conclusion that area 11 links visual inputs with updated values (C93) is well-supported by the experimental data. The comparison to human fMRI (C90-C92) provides converging evidence. The speculation about area 12 involvement (C94) is appropriately tentative and supported by relevant citations about area 12 function.

results.result: West et al. (2011) found that OFC inactivation disrupted both value updating and goal selection, likely because their central infusions affected both areas 11 and 13 simultaneously.
results.evaluation: The comparison to West et al. (C95) and explanation for differing results (C96) is reasonable and well-argued. The anatomical explanation for the discrepancy is plausible, though other methodological differences (species, stimuli, drug) are appropriately acknowledged as potential factors.

results.result: Anatomical evidence suggests hierarchical organization with feedforward projections from area 11 to area 13. Visual representations in area 11 may activate posterior areas for integration with value signals, with other regions (area 12, anterior insula) providing redundant value information.
results.evaluation: The anatomical claims (C97-C99) are supported by appropriate citations. However, the functional model (C100) and proposed redundancy (C101) are speculative interpretations not directly tested by the current experiments. The model is plausible but would require additional experiments (e.g., simultaneous inactivation, connectivity studies) to validate.

results.result: The OFC influences behavior through connections to motor systems, potentially via serial value comparison or biased competition mechanisms. Anatomical pathways through ventral, medial, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to premotor areas provide routes for value-based action selection.
results.evaluation: The general principle (C102) is logically sound. The presentation of alternative models (C103-C104) is appropriate and well-cited. The anatomical pathways (C105-C108) are supported by relevant citations. However, the current data do not distinguish between the proposed mechanisms, making this primarily a framework for future investigation rather than a tested conclusion.

results.result: Prior work establishes that frontal lobe damage disrupts translation of knowledge into action, a phenomenon termed goal neglect. This deficit can occur in isolation and may be fundamental to various psychopathologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C14 accurately represent prior literature with appropriate citations to classic neuropsychological studies. The speculative extension to psychopathologies (C15) is appropriately tentative. These claims establish the theoretical context for the study but do not constitute new findings.

results.result: Prior work demonstrates that the amygdala and OFC (particularly areas 11 and 13) are necessary for devaluation effects and must functionally interact. Neurons in both areas signal expected outcome values, but functional specializations within the OFC were previously unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C27 accurately summarize relevant prior literature with appropriate citations. These establish the knowledge gap (C26-C27) that motivates the current study. The citations appear accurate and the synthesis is fair, though the authors should verify that cited work actually supports the specific claims made.

results.result: The macaque OFC is essential for selecting goals based on current, updated values of expected outcomes. OFC damage impairs the ability to shift choices away from devalued outcomes after selective satiation.
results.evaluation: These foundational claims (C1-C2) are supported by the experimental results and prior literature. However, they represent general background rather than novel findings from this study. The specific contributions are the dissociation between areas 11 and 13 documented in other result groups.

results.result: Saline control infusions produced robust devaluation effects, with monkeys shifting choices toward images associated with higher-value (nonsated) outcomes after selective satiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 document the expected control condition behavior illustrated in Figure 4. These results confirm that the task and satiation procedure work as intended, providing the baseline against which drug effects are measured. Essential for interpretation but not a novel finding.

results.result: A significant three-way interaction between Treatment, Region, and Time (F(1,4)=16.82, p=0.015, partial η²=0.81) indicates that inactivation effects differed by both brain area and timing relative to satiation.
results.evaluation: The statistical result (C44) is clearly reported with appropriate test statistics and effect size. The three-way interaction is the key statistical finding supporting the double dissociation. However, with only n=5 subjects, power is limited and the result should be interpreted cautiously despite the large effect size.

results.result: The complementary functions of areas 11 and 13 agree with the concept of an orbitomedial prefrontal sensory network. Updated values are stored during/after satiation (area 13-dependent) and broadcast to area 11 for goal selection.
results.evaluation: The integration with the sensory network framework (C63) is appropriate and well-cited. The proposed mechanism (C71-C72) is a reasonable interpretation of the timing-dependent effects, though C72 is explicitly speculative about storage and transmission mechanisms. The model is plausible but not directly tested.
